newsitem.title: EGYPT: Police brutality Egyptian way of life - rights group.
newsitem.headline: Police brutality Egyptian way of life - rights group.

text.p: A human rights group said legal loopholes have increased police brutality in Egypt, with torture and killing of detainees a way of life for many in the force.

In a report made available on Tuesday, the Egyptian Organisation for Human Rights (EOHR) said torture and maltreatment was "widescale and systematic policy practised by officers during interrogation of suspects and detainees in police stations."

"The phenomenon has reached tragic proportions," the report said. "It has become so prevalent and normal inside most police stations and squads... and unfortunately the authorities have not yet taken any steps to end this."
The Egyptian Interior Ministry referred questions to the Foreign Ministry's Human Rights Department, where the official responsible was unavailable.
The group noted the Egyptian constitution said every citizen detained must be treated with respect, but said other laws allow the police to use violence.
"There is a dangerous lack of legal guarantees for detainees inside police stations, which allow police officers to flout the constitution," the report said.

"Among them is an article in the law which allows police to arrest a person if there is 'sufficient evidence' against them. The term is too vague and allows police to detain without a warrant," it added.
They said victims could not take police torturers to court because the law says "persons involved in fighting a crime are not liable for their actions on duty".
Other loopholes include insufficient definition of torture and the use of emergency law, which allows police to detain people without charge for unlimited lengths of time.

Egyptians complain of police brutality even in cases with no political significance. Last year two journalists told Reuters at least eight policemen beat them with rifle butts after they argued over a broken tail-light.
In political cases police abuses are routine, say relatives of people suspected to be militant Islamists.

"When they were looking for my son, I would spend almost every night in the police station. They would swear at me, spit in my face, beat and punch me, have me kneel on the floor and electrocute me to tell them where he is," the mother of a convicted Moslem militant told Reuters outside a courtroom.
The EOHR report documented 52 cases of police brutality in which 12 people died in custody.

"People are tortured to confess to certain crimes, their families are taken hostage to force them to confess, they are beaten up as a compliment to influential people or for simply no reason at all," the report said.
Methods of torture include hanging the bound victim like "meat on a hook", electrocution, beating with sticks, burning, and raping women, the report said.

"The government must set up an independent body to investigate all allegations of torture and it must set up immediate awareness courses for police officers. The laws must also be amended," the group said.
